_README: Hand-written for this project. NOT adapted from any licensed third-party source, and
not from the BSB — only the section headings come from there.
Drawn from plain historical fact and public-domain reference works (Matthew
Henry's Commentary, 1710; the Scofield Reference Bible, 1909).
Shipped under DATA_PROFILE=public. Add books freely — a book with no entry
here simply renders without an introduction.
Voice: for someone about to read the book who may never have read it before.
Say what it is, when it was written, what it is doing, and what a reader will
actually meet in it. No exhortation, no selling. Two short paragraphs.
PROVENANCE: every intro records who drafted it and what they had been exposed
to. See _provenance below and src/data/sections/SOURCE.md. Eight books are
reserved for the owner because an assistant had already read a licensed
introductions for them in the session where the PDFs were ingested, and a
no-shared-sentence check cannot detect borrowed structure or emphasis.

ruth:
Ruth is four chapters long and set during the time of the judges, a period the book of Judges describes as lawless and grim. It opens with a famine, a family leaving Bethlehem for Moab, and three deaths in quick succession — and then narrows to two widows walking back to Bethlehem with nothing. Ruth, the younger, is a Moabitess, a foreigner from a people Israel had every historical reason to distrust.

What follows is an ordinary story: gleaning in a barley field, a landowner's kindness, a legal transaction at the town gate about who has the right to redeem a dead man's property and marry his widow. It is told without miracles and almost without mention of God acting directly. The last five verses reveal why it was kept: Ruth becomes the great-grandmother of David. In Jewish tradition it is read at Shavuot, the festival of the harvest it describes.
jonah:
Jonah is the odd one out among the prophets. The other prophetic books are collections of oracles — what the prophet said. Jonah is a story about the prophet himself, and he comes off badly in nearly all of it. Four short chapters: a commission refused, a storm, a fish, a reluctant sermon, and an argument with God that the book simply stops in the middle of.

Jonah is named in 2 Kings 14:25 as a prophet under Jeroboam II, which places him in the eighth century BC. Nineveh was the great city of Assyria — the empire that would destroy the northern kingdom within his century — so his refusal to go is not cowardice so much as a refusal to see that city spared. That is what the closing chapter is about, and it ends on a question God asks Jonah, which the book never answers. The reader is left holding it.
ecclesiastes:
Ecclesiastes is the most unguarded book in the Bible. Its speaker calls himself Qoheleth — usually rendered "the Preacher" or "the Teacher" — and he has tried everything: work, pleasure, learning, building, wealth. His verdict on all of it is the word the King James translates "vanity", which in Hebrew is *hevel*: vapour, breath, something you cannot get hold of. He uses it nearly forty times.

It belongs to the wisdom literature, alongside Proverbs and Job, and it argues with Proverbs more than it agrees. Where Proverbs says the diligent prosper, Ecclesiastes notes that the same fate meets the wise and the fool, and that a man's heirs may squander everything he built. It does not resolve this. Readers have found it bleak and readers have found it the only honest book they own; both are reading it correctly. It ends by telling you to fear God and keep his commandments, having spent twelve chapters refusing to pretend that this makes life legible.
philippians:
Paul wrote Philippians from prison, probably in Rome in the early 60s AD, to a church he had founded himself about ten years earlier. Acts 16 tells that founding: a riverside prayer meeting, a businesswoman named Lydia, a girl delivered from a spirit of divination, and a night in the Philippian jail that ended with the jailer baptised. Philippi was a Roman colony, and its Christians were the first in Europe.

The letter is warm in a way Paul's letters often are not. He is not correcting a crisis here; he is thanking them for money they sent, explaining his situation, and asking them to stop quarrelling — two women are named. Chapter two carries what is probably an early Christian hymn about Christ emptying himself, quoted rather than composed for the occasion. Paul writes repeatedly about joy, from a cell, without explaining the contradiction.
james:
James reads less like a letter than like the wisdom books of the Old Testament — short, blunt, practical, moving quickly between subjects without connecting them. It has more imperatives per line than anything else in the New Testament. The author is traditionally identified as James the brother of Jesus, who led the Jerusalem church and is named in Acts 15 presiding over the council there.

Its concerns are consistent: what people do with money, what they do with their tongues, and how they treat the poor when nobody is watching. The passage on faith and works in chapter two has been argued over since the Reformation, when Luther called the book an epistle of straw for it. Read next to Paul it looks like a contradiction; read on its own terms it is asking a narrower question — not how a person is saved, but how you would tell.
exodus:
Exodus picks up about four hundred years after Genesis ends, with Joseph's family grown into a people and enslaved by a Pharaoh who "knew not Joseph". It covers two things: a rescue, and what the rescued were then asked to become. The first half is the famous half — the burning bush, the plagues, the Passover, the sea opening — and it moves fast.

The second half slows to a halt, and readers often stop there. After Sinai the book turns to law and then to architecture: the Ten Commandments, then chapters of case law, then detailed specifications for a portable tent and its furnishings, given once as instruction and repeated almost verbatim as a record that it was built. The repetition is the point. A people who had just been property are given, in exhaustive detail, something of their own to make.
leviticus:
Leviticus is the book most reading plans die in. It is almost entirely instruction — sacrifices, priesthood, clean and unclean, festivals, land — delivered with little narrative to carry a reader along. Its two stories are both brief and both grim.

It rewards being read as a manual for a particular people at a particular moment: newly freed, camped around a tent, working out what it means that God is living in the middle of them. Nearly everything in it turns on that one problem. The word "holy" appears more here than anywhere else in the Bible, and it means set apart rather than morally superior. Chapter 19 is the one most readers know without knowing where it is from: love thy neighbour as thyself, sitting in the middle of rules about harvesting and wages and not cursing the deaf.
numbers:
Numbers takes its English name from the two censuses that open and close it — one generation counted at Sinai, another counted forty years later on the plains of Moab. Almost everyone in the first list dies before the second. That is the book's argument in its structure: this is what happened to the generation that came out of Egypt.

What fills the space between is the wilderness, and it is mostly complaint. Food, water, leadership, the report of the spies who said the land could not be taken. Twelve went in, two came back willing. Numbers also holds some of the strangest material in the Old Testament — a bronze serpent, a talking donkey, a foreign prophet hired to curse Israel who blesses it instead — and one of its most familiar passages, the blessing of chapter 6: the LORD bless thee, and keep thee.
deuteronomy:
Deuteronomy is one long farewell. Moses is a hundred and twenty years old, standing east of the Jordan with a people he will not cross it with, and the book is essentially three sermons and a song. Its name means "second law" — it retells and reapplies what was given at Sinai, to a generation that was not there.

It is the most quoted Old Testament book in the New. The Shema is here — hear, O Israel, the LORD our God is one LORD — and so is the command to love God with all your heart, which Jesus calls the first commandment. Jesus answers all three wilderness temptations with lines from it. The book ends with Moses seeing the land from Mount Nebo and dying there, and the note that no one knows where he is buried.
joshua:
Joshua covers a single generation and one task: crossing into the land and taking it. The first half is campaign — Jericho, Ai, a long day at Gibeon — and the second half is surveying, dividing the territory tribe by tribe with the precision of a land registry.

It is the book modern readers most often find hard, and it is worth knowing that going in rather than being surprised by it. The conquest accounts are written in the idiom of ancient war reporting, sweeping and total in their language, and the same book that says a region was wholly taken later describes the people still living there. Its closing scene is the one most often remembered: Joshua, old, gathering the tribes at Shechem and making them choose out loud — as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
judges:
Judges covers roughly three centuries between Joshua's death and the first king, and it gets darker as it goes. The pattern repeats: the people drift, an enemy oppresses them, they cry out, God raises up a deliverer — a "judge", meaning a military leader rather than a magistrate — and there is peace until that judge dies. Then it begins again, worse.

The judges themselves are an uneven collection: Deborah, who governs and goes to war; Gideon, who needs three signs before he will believe; Jephthah, who makes a vow that costs him his daughter; Samson, who is more a force of nature than a leader. The last chapters abandon the pattern for two atrocities told without comment, and the book's final sentence is its verdict on the whole period: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
1-samuel:
First Samuel is about the arrival of kingship and what it cost. It opens with a barren woman praying at the tabernacle and closes with a king dead on a battlefield, and it turns on three figures: Samuel, the last of the judges; Saul, the first king; and David, the shepherd anointed while Saul still reigns.

The people ask for a king so they can be like the other nations, and Samuel warns them at length what a king will take. They ask anyway. Saul begins well and unravels, and much of the second half is a long pursuit — Saul hunting David through the wilderness while David, twice able to kill him, does not. The famous scenes are here: the boy hearing his name in the night, the anointing of the youngest son nobody thought to call in from the sheep, and David and Goliath.
2-samuel:
Second Samuel is David's reign, and it divides cleanly at chapter 11. Before it, almost everything goes right: the tribes united, Jerusalem taken and made the capital, the ark brought up with David dancing before it, and a promise that his house and kingdom will be established for ever.

After it, almost nothing does. The adultery with Bathsheba and the arranged death of her husband are told plainly, with none of the softening a court history would normally apply to its own king, and the consequences run through the rest of the book: a child's death, a daughter raped, a son murdered, and finally Absalom's rebellion and David fleeing his own city barefoot. The book is remarkable partly for what it refuses to hide about the man it plainly admires.
1-kings:
First Kings opens with Solomon, and the early chapters are the high-water mark of the whole Old Testament story: a young king asking for wisdom rather than wealth, the temple built and filled, a foreign queen coming to see whether the reports are true. Then the same king accumulates wives, horses and foreign altars, and the account turns cold.

After his death the kingdom splits — ten tribes north under Jeroboam, two south under Rehoboam — and the book settles into a rhythm of paired reigns, each king given a short verdict on whether he did right or evil. Into that comes Elijah, and the pace changes entirely: the drought, the ravens, the widow's jar of meal, the confrontation on Carmel, and then the collapse afterwards in the desert, where God is not in the wind or the earthquake or the fire but in a still small voice.
2-kings:
Second Kings carries the two kingdoms to their ends. It opens with Elijah taken up in a whirlwind and Elisha asking for a double portion of his spirit, and the Elisha chapters that follow hold some of the most domestic miracles in scripture — a borrowed axe head, a poisoned pot of stew, oil that keeps pouring while there are jars to fill.

Then the record grinds on through the kings, and the verdicts get worse. Samaria falls to Assyria in 722 BC and the northern kingdom simply stops. Judah lasts another century and a half, with two genuine reforms under Hezekiah and Josiah, before Babylon comes. The book ends with Jerusalem burned, the temple stripped, the people deported, and a last small note: the exiled king of Judah released from prison in Babylon and given a seat at the table. It is not resolution, but it is not nothing.
1-chronicles:
First Chronicles retells material a reader has already met in Samuel and Kings, and the interesting question is what it leaves out. It was compiled after the exile, for people who had come back to a ruined city and needed to know whether they were still the same nation. The first nine chapters are genealogy — from Adam forward — and they are there to answer exactly that.

The rest is David, but a narrower David than the one in Second Samuel. Bathsheba is absent. So is Absalom's rebellion, and the long decline. What the Chronicler keeps is the ark brought to Jerusalem, the organisation of the Levites and the singers, and David spending his last years gathering materials and drawing plans for a temple he is told he will not build. The book ends with him handing those plans to Solomon in front of the whole assembly.
2-chronicles:
Second Chronicles runs from Solomon's temple to the fall of Jerusalem, and then adds four verses that change the ending. It follows the kings of Judah only; the northern kingdom appears when it intersects with the south and is otherwise left to Kings. The temple is the organising interest throughout — built, filled, neglected, plundered, repaired, cleansed, and finally burned.

Its best-known passages are the reform narratives, where a king reopens the doors his father shut: Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah keeping a Passover so late that the northern remnant is invited to it, and Josiah finding the book of the law during building work. The ending is the reason the Hebrew Bible places Chronicles last. Jerusalem falls, the land lies desolate for seventy years, and then Cyrus of Persia issues a decree — and the book stops mid-proclamation, on the word "go up".
ezra:
Ezra begins where Chronicles stops, with the decree of Cyrus in 538 BC, and covers two returns from Babylon separated by about eighty years. The first, under Zerubbabel and Jeshua, rebuilds the altar and lays a foundation; the work then halts for years under local opposition and imperial correspondence, and resumes only when Haggai and Zechariah start preaching. The second temple is finished in 516 BC.

Ezra himself does not appear until chapter seven. He is a scribe, expert in the law of Moses, and he arrives with a royal commission and a second group of returnees. Some of the book is in Aramaic rather than Hebrew — the language of Persian administration, used for the documents it quotes. It ends abruptly and unhappily, with Ezra confronting intermarriage among the returned community, and a list of names. In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah are a single book.
nehemiah:
Nehemiah is written largely in the first person, which makes it unusual. Its author is cupbearer to Artaxerxes in the Persian capital when news reaches him that Jerusalem's wall is still broken down a century after the first return. He asks for leave, gets it, and the book becomes an account of a building project conducted under harassment — night inspections, work rotas, families assigned to the section of wall nearest their own houses, and a standing guard.

The wall takes fifty-two days. Then the book changes character: Ezra reads the law aloud from a wooden platform at the Water Gate from morning until midday, with Levites moving through the crowd explaining it, and the people weep. What follows is a covenant signed by name, a repopulating of the city, and Nehemiah's second term, in which he returns to find the reforms lapsed and deals with it bluntly. The last verse is a request that God remember him.
esther:
Esther never mentions God. It is the only book in the Hebrew Bible that does not, and readers have argued about that for two thousand years. It is set entirely in the Persian empire, in the citadel of Susa, in the reign of Ahasuerus — the king the Greeks called Xerxes — and it reads like court history: banquets, protocol, insomnia, and the exact wording of edicts that cannot be revoked once sealed.

The plot turns on reversals. A queen is deposed for refusing to appear and a Jewish orphan takes her place without disclosing who she is. Haman builds a gallows for Mordecai and is hanged on it. A decree to destroy the Jews on a date chosen by lot is answered by a second decree permitting them to defend themselves. The feast of Purim takes its name from that lot, and Esther is read aloud at it each year, in full, with the congregation drowning out Haman's name.
job:
Job is a poem with a story wrapped around it. The prose opening and closing are plain and quick; everything between chapters three and forty-two is verse, and it is some of the most difficult Hebrew in the Bible. Job is not an Israelite and the land of Uz is not in Israel. No covenant, no temple, no law — the book is deliberately set outside all of that.

The question is not whether Job sinned. The reader is told in the first chapter that he did not, which the characters never learn. Three friends come to sit with him, say nothing for seven days, and then spend some twenty-five chapters arguing that suffering of this kind has a cause and he should admit it. Job refuses, and keeps demanding a hearing. When God finally answers out of the whirlwind, it is with questions rather than explanations — about weather, wild animals, the sea, and two creatures described at length. Job is restored at the end. He is never told why.
proverbs:
Proverbs is not one book but several collections bound together, and it helps to know which one you are in. Chapters one to nine are sustained speeches — a father to a son, and Wisdom herself personified as a woman calling in the street. From chapter ten the form changes to single couplets, hundreds of them, largely unconnected, each complete in a line. Later sections are attributed to unnamed wise men, to Agur, and to King Lemuel's mother.

One group is introduced as proverbs of Solomon "which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out" — a note about editing, three centuries after Solomon, left in the text. The sayings are general truths about how life usually goes rather than promises about how it always will; Job and Ecclesiastes are in the same Bible partly to say so. The final chapter is an acrostic poem, twenty-two verses running through the Hebrew alphabet, describing a woman who buys fields and trades and is not afraid of the snow.
jeremiah:
Jeremiah prophesied for about forty years, from the reign of Josiah through the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC and into the aftermath, and almost nobody listened. He was from Anathoth, a priestly village a few miles from Jerusalem, and his own townsmen plotted against him. His message — that Babylon would take the city and resistance was futile — was heard as treason, and he was beaten, put in the stocks, imprisoned and lowered into a cistern for it.

The book is not in chronological order, which surprises readers who expect a narrative. It moves between oracles, sermons, biography, and passages often called the confessions, where Jeremiah complains to God in language nobody else in scripture uses. It contains the temple sermon, the potter's house, the seventy years, a scroll that Jehoiakim cut up and burned page by page, and the promise of a new covenant written on the heart. He is last seen in Egypt, taken there against his will by the people he stayed behind with.
lamentations:
Lamentations is five poems about the destruction of Jerusalem, and they are formally strict in a way that is invisible in English. Chapters one, two and four each have twenty-two verses beginning with the successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Chapter three has sixty-six — three verses per letter. Chapter five has twenty-two verses and abandons the acrostic altogether, which is the point at which the form gives way.

What it describes is siege and its aftermath: famine, the temple entered, children asking for bread, a city that was full of people sitting alone. It does not soften any of this or hurry past it. At the exact centre, in the tightest of the five poems, comes the passage everyone knows — his compassions fail not, they are new every morning — and then the lament resumes. Jewish tradition reads the whole book on Tisha B'Av, the fast that marks the day the temple fell.
ezekiel:
Ezekiel was a priest, deported to Babylon in 597 BC in the wave before the city finally fell, and he prophesied by an irrigation canal called the Chebar among other exiles. He dates his visions precisely, which makes his book one of the easiest to place in time and one of the strangest to read. It opens with a vision of a storm out of the north, four living creatures, wheels within wheels, and a throne above them.

Much of what he was told to do he had to perform rather than say: lie on one side for months, shave his head and divide the hair three ways, pack a bag and dig through a wall at dusk while people watched. Chapters eight to eleven describe the glory of God leaving the temple by stages, which is the hinge of the book. After Jerusalem falls the tone changes from warning to restoration — the shepherds, the valley of dry bones, a new heart of flesh — and it closes with nine chapters of measurements for a temple that has never been built, and a city whose name is "the LORD is there".
daniel:
Daniel divides in half and changes both person and language as it goes. Chapters one to six are stories told about Daniel — the refused food, the dream of a statue made of four metals, the furnace, the writing on the wall, the lions' den — and they are set in the courts of Babylon and then Persia, where a deported Judean youth rises to high office under kings who keep changing. Chapters seven to twelve are visions Daniel reports in the first person, and they are far harder going.

A long stretch in the middle, from the second chapter to the end of the seventh, is written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew — the working language of the empire — and it is the section most concerned with foreign kings. The visions that follow use beasts, horns and numbered periods to describe kingdoms rising and falling, and the interpretation of them has been contested for two thousand years. What is not contested is the pressure the book describes: how to serve a government that periodically requires you to stop being who you are.
hosea:
Hosea prophesied in the northern kingdom in its last decades, while it still looked prosperous, and the book is built on his own marriage. He is told to take a wife who will be unfaithful, and the children are given names that are messages in themselves: Jezreel, after a massacre; Lo-ruhamah, not pitied; Lo-ammi, not my people. Then he is told to go and love her again after she has left.

The rest is oracle, and the Hebrew is among the most difficult in the Old Testament — compressed, abrupt, switching between tenderness and fury without transition. The charge is that Israel has treated its covenant the way Gomer treated her marriage, and that the political manoeuvring between Egypt and Assyria is of a piece with it. Two lines are quoted in the New Testament: out of Egypt have I called my son, and I desired mercy and not sacrifice, which Jesus tells his critics twice to go and learn the meaning of.
joel:
Joel opens with a locust swarm. Wave after wave has stripped the land bare — the book names four kinds of locust in a single verse — and the grain offering and drink offering have stopped because there is nothing left to offer. The priests are told to put on sackcloth and call a fast, and the elders are asked whether anything like this has happened in their lifetime or their fathers'.

From there it widens. The locusts become an image for an invading army, and the invading army for the day of the LORD, a phrase Joel uses more than anyone. It is only three chapters and it does not say who was king or what year it was, which is why its date is argued over more than most. Two passages are widely known: rend your heart, and not your garments, and the promise that God will pour out his spirit upon all flesh — which Peter stands up and quotes at Pentecost as the explanation of what has just happened.
amos:
Amos was not a professional prophet and says so: a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah who also tended sycomore figs, sent north to Israel around 760 BC, during a long reign of real prosperity. That prosperity is his subject. He describes ivory houses, winter houses and summer houses, beds of ivory, and the people who paid for them — sold for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes.

He opens with a sequence of oracles against the surrounding nations, each in the same form, and an Israelite audience would have enjoyed the first seven. The eighth is about them. The priest at Bethel eventually tells him to go home and prophesy where he came from. The book is remembered for two lines in particular — let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream; and the warning that God hates their feast days and will not hear the melody of their viols while that is going on.
obadiah:
Obadiah is the shortest book in the Old Testament: twenty-one verses, one chapter, a single subject. It is addressed to Edom, the nation descended from Esau, Jacob's brother — and the family relationship is the whole point of it.

The charge is not that Edom attacked Jerusalem but that it stood by and watched, looked on while strangers carried away the city's wealth, and then cut off those who tried to escape. "Thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother" is the line the book turns on. Edom's territory was high rock country, and Obadiah plays on that throughout: you who dwell in the clefts of the rock, who says in his heart, who shall bring me down. It ends in four verses that widen from Edom to the whole day of the LORD.
micah:
Micah came from Moresheth, a country town in the lowlands rather than the capital, and prophesied at the same time as Isaiah, to both kingdoms, in the years before Samaria fell. His complaints are specific and local: men who covet fields and seize them, judges who take a bribe, prophets who preach peace to whoever feeds them, merchants with two sets of weights.

For a short book it holds an unusual number of familiar lines. The vision of nations beating swords into plowshares appears here and in Isaiah in nearly the same words. Bethlehem Ephratah, little among the thousands of Judah, is named as the place a ruler will come from. And chapter six puts the whole question of what God wants into a single sentence — to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God. A century later, when Jeremiah was on trial for his life, elders cited Micah as the precedent that saved him.
nahum:
Nahum is about Nineveh, the same city Jonah was sent to, roughly a century and a half later. In Jonah the city repents and is spared. In Nahum there is no offer and no reprieve — only a description of what is about to happen to the capital of the empire that had destroyed the northern kingdom and besieged Jerusalem. It fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC.

The book is three chapters of sustained poetry and it is written to be heard. The second chapter reads like an eyewitness account of a city being taken: the shield of his mighty men is made red, the chariots rage in the streets, the gates of the rivers are opened. Readers who come to it looking for comfort tend to find it uncomfortable. It was written for people who had been on the receiving end of Assyria for a hundred years, and it says that empires are not permanent.
habakkuk:
Habakkuk is a conversation rather than a sermon. The prophet begins by complaining — how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear — about violence and injustice going unanswered in Judah. God replies that he is raising up the Chaldeans, and the answer is worse than the question: Habakkuk's second complaint is that using a crueller nation to punish a less cruel one solves nothing. Then he climbs the watchtower to wait and see what will be said to him.

The answer he is given includes the line that the just shall live by his faith, which Paul quotes in Romans and Galatians and the letter to the Hebrews quotes again — one short clause from a minor prophet carrying an enormous amount of later weight. The third chapter is a psalm, complete with musical directions, and it ends with a statement of trust made in the absence of everything: though the fig tree shall not blossom and there be no herd in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the LORD.
zephaniah:
Zephaniah's first verse traces his ancestry back four generations, to Hezekiah, which is unusual for a prophet and suggests royal blood. He prophesied under Josiah, the king who carried out the last great reform, and the corruption he describes — priests, princes, judges, prophets — is probably what that reform was aimed at.

The book is dominated by the day of the LORD, described in terms so severe that the Latin of one verse gave the medieval requiem its opening words. Zephaniah sweeps outward to the surrounding nations and back to Jerusalem, and then, in the last dozen verses, changes completely. The closing passage is one of the warmest in the prophets: a promise that God will save the lame and gather the outcast, and will rejoice over his people with singing.
haggai:
Haggai is two chapters long and dated to the day. Four messages, delivered over roughly four months in 520 BC, to people who had come back from exile eighteen years earlier, started rebuilding the temple, been stopped, and never resumed. His question is simply why: is it time for you to dwell in your panelled houses, and this house lie waste?

They begin work twenty-three days after the first message, which makes Haggai one of the few prophets in the Bible whose audience did what he said. The second message deals with the disappointment that followed — some of those watching were old enough to have seen Solomon's temple, and this one looked like nothing beside it. Haggai's answer is that the glory of the latter house shall be greater than of the former. The book ends with a promise to Zerubbabel, the governor descended from David.
zechariah:
Zechariah began prophesying two months after Haggai, to the same people and about the same building project, but the manner could hardly be more different. Where Haggai is plain and practical, Zechariah opens with eight visions in a single night — a man among myrtle trees, four horns, a measuring line, a flying scroll, a woman in a basket carried off by storks, four chariots between mountains of brass — each explained by an angel who has to be asked. One of them shows the high priest standing in filthy garments and being given clean ones, and another produces the line that is quoted more than any other: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.

The last six chapters change style so completely that they are often treated as a separate collection. They are harder, stranger and more distant, and they contain a remarkable number of the details the Gospel writers reach for when they describe the final week: a king coming lowly and riding upon an ass, thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter, a shepherd struck and the sheep scattered, and a city looking on one whom they have pierced.
malachi:
Malachi is the last book of the Old Testament in Christian Bibles, and it is set a long way down from the drama of the exile — perhaps a century after the return, with the temple rebuilt and the enthusiasm gone. Its subject is that flatness. The sacrifices being offered are the animals nobody wanted: blind, lame, sick. The priests are bored. The name means "my messenger", and whether it is a name at all is disputed.

The book is built as a series of arguments. God makes a charge, the people answer with a question — wherein have we despised thy name? wherein have we robbed thee? — and the charge is then spelled out. There are six of these, and they cover worship, marriage and divorce, and the tithe, where the answer includes the only invitation in scripture to put God to the test. It ends by promising that Elijah will come before the great and dreadful day of the LORD, and the Old Testament closes on that unfinished note.
2-corinthians:
Second Corinthians is the least orderly and most personal of Paul's letters. It comes after a visit that went badly and a letter written, as he puts it, out of much affliction and anguish of heart with many tears — a letter we do not have. Much of what he writes here is relief: Titus has come back with news that the church took the rebuke well.

The rest is a defence of his own standing, forced on him by rival teachers he calls, with heavy sarcasm, the very chiefest apostles. Because they boast of credentials, he boasts too, and the list he produces is of beatings, shipwrecks, sleeplessness, hunger, and the daily weight of the churches — followed by the thorn in the flesh he asked three times to have removed and was not given. Two chapters in the middle are about money: a collection he is gathering from Gentile churches for the poor in Jerusalem, and the tact with which he asks for it.
galatians:
Galatians is the one letter of Paul's that skips the thanksgiving. He goes straight from the greeting to astonishment that his readers have abandoned what he taught them, and the temperature does not drop for six chapters. The issue is whether Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to belong, and he treats it as a question about whether the gospel survives at all.

The first two chapters are autobiography, given as evidence: how he received his message, how long it was before he met the Jerusalem apostles, and the occasion at Antioch when he opposed Peter to his face for withdrawing from Gentile tables. From there he argues from Abraham, from the law's purpose, and from the status of an heir. The last section turns to conduct and gives the list most readers know — love, joy, peace, longsuffering — and he signs off by pointing out how large the letters are in the part he has written with his own hand.
ephesians:
Ephesians is the calmest of the letters attributed to Paul and the least tied to a local crisis. The words "at Ephesus" are missing from the earliest manuscripts, which has led many to read it as a circular letter meant to be carried from church to church. Nothing in it addresses a named dispute or a particular person's conduct.

It divides neatly in half. The first three chapters are about what God has done — beginning with a passage that runs as a single unbroken sentence in the Greek — and the central image is a wall pulled down: two peoples who had no dealings with each other made into one. The last three are about how that is lived, and they move from speech and anger and honest work through instructions to husbands, wives, children and slaves, to the closing picture of armour, piece by piece, which is where most readers' memory of the book begins and ends.
colossians:
Colossians was written to a church Paul had never visited. Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley, and the gospel had reached it through Epaphras, who came to Paul in prison with a report. Something was being taught there that combined Jewish observance with asceticism and a preoccupation with angelic powers, and Paul's answer is not to refute it point by point but to say what he thinks Christ actually is.

That answer is concentrated in a passage near the start — the image of the invisible God, firstborn of every creature, by whom all things consist — which reads like a hymn and may have been one before he quoted it. The practical half warns against being judged over meat and drink and holy days, and then gives the ordinary instructions: put off anger, put on kindness, sing, be thankful. It travelled with Tychicus, alongside the short personal note we have as Philemon, and the same runaway slave is mentioned in both.
1-thessalonians:
First Thessalonians is very likely the oldest document in the New Testament, written around AD 50, within months of the visit Acts 17 describes — a few weeks of preaching in the synagogue, a riot, and Paul leaving town at night. He had not wanted to leave, and the letter is what he writes after Timothy finally gets back to him with news that the church survived.

It corrects almost nothing. Most of it is relief, affection, and a defence of his motives against whatever was being said about him after he left. The section readers come for is near the end, and it answers a specific worry: members of the church had died, and those left behind wanted to know whether they had missed something. Paul's reply — that the dead in Christ shall rise first, and that the day comes as a thief in the night — is the earliest written account we have of what the first Christians expected.
2-thessalonians:
Second Thessalonians is shorter than the first letter, and noticeably cooler. The affection is still there but the occasion is a problem: someone has been saying that the day of the Lord has already come, and the claim has been attached to Paul's own name — by spirit, by word, or by letter as from us.

So he writes to deny it, and to say what must happen first. That middle chapter, with its restraining force and its man of sin, is among the most debated passages in the New Testament, and he assumes his readers remember an explanation he gave them in person which we do not have. The last chapter deals with the practical fallout: people who had stopped working, apparently because they thought there was no point. His instruction is blunt, and he offers his own trade as the precedent — if any would not work, neither should he eat. He signs this one himself, so that they will know the next letter is genuine.
1-timothy:
First Timothy is one of three letters written to individuals rather than congregations, and it reads like a set of standing orders. Timothy has been left at Ephesus with a specific job: to stop certain people teaching things Paul describes as endless genealogies and profane babblings, and to put the church's ordinary life in order.

Most of the letter is therefore practical to the point of being administrative — what to look for in an overseer or a deacon, how to handle a charge against an elder, which widows the church should support and which have families who should be supporting them, how to speak to older and younger men and women. It also carries one of the most misquoted lines in the Bible: not that money is the root of all evil, but the love of it. Whether Paul wrote these three letters himself or they were assembled later from his instructions is one of the long-running questions of New Testament scholarship.
2-timothy:
Second Timothy reads like a last letter, and has been treated as one since the early church. Paul is in prison again, and this time he is not expecting release: he describes himself as already being poured out, and says that at his first defence no one stood with him. Demas has left. Only Luke is there.

It is short and largely personal, and it moves between charges to Timothy — preach the word, endure affliction, keep the pattern of sound words — and small domestic requests that are the reason many readers find it the most affecting of the letters. He asks Timothy to come before winter, and to bring the cloak he left at Troas, and the books, and especially the parchments. It also contains the sentence that has framed every argument about the Bible since: all scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable.
titus:
Titus is the shortest of the three letters written to individuals, and its setting is unusual: Crete, where Titus has been left to appoint elders in every town in a church that is evidently very new. Paul quotes a Cretan poet's insult about his own countrymen and says it is true, which has made the letter awkward reading ever since.

Almost everything in it is about credibility. The qualifications for an elder are about character rather than ability. The instructions to older men, older women, younger women, young men and slaves all end with the same kind of reason — so that the teaching is not discredited by the people holding it. Twice the letter breaks into what reads like quoted creed, and the second of those passages contains the line about the kindness and love of God our Saviour appearing, not by works of righteousness which we have done.
philemon:
Philemon is a single page: twenty-five verses, one subject, and the only private letter of Paul's that has survived. Onesimus, a slave belonging to a Christian named Philemon, has run away and somehow ended up with Paul in prison, where he has become a believer. Paul is sending him back, and the letter is what he sends with him.

It is a careful piece of writing. Paul says explicitly that he could command and is choosing to ask. He offers to pay whatever Onesimus owes, writing the promissory line in his own hand, and then reminds Philemon in passing what he already owes Paul. He asks that Onesimus be received not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved — and stops short of saying the word he is plainly circling. What Philemon did is not recorded. The letter was kept, which may be an answer.
hebrews:
Hebrews does not say who wrote it, and the early church did not know either. It has no greeting, opens like a sermon rather than a letter, and closes with personal notes that sound like one. The Greek is the most polished in the New Testament. Its readers are Jewish Christians under pressure and apparently considering going back, and the whole book is an argument that there is nothing to go back to that is not already here in better form.

It works through a sequence of comparisons — better than the angels, than Moses, than Aaron, than the sacrifices — and leans heavily on the tabernacle described in Exodus and Leviticus, which makes it hard going for readers who have skipped those. Interleaved with the argument are five sharp warnings against drifting away. The eleventh chapter is the one everyone knows: a roll-call of people who were commended for their faith and, the chapter is careful to say, did not receive what was promised.
1-peter:
First Peter is addressed to scattered believers across five provinces of what is now Turkey, and it calls them strangers and pilgrims — resident foreigners, people living somewhere that is not home. That image governs the letter. They are suffering, though from social hostility and slander rather than any state persecution the letter names, and Peter's question is how to live well in a place that has decided against you.

His answer is not withdrawal. He tells them to be subject to the emperor, to masters, to husbands, and to be ready always to give an answer to anyone who asks a reason for the hope in them — with meekness and fear. Christ's own suffering is held up throughout as the pattern, in language drawn from the servant of Isaiah 53. The letter says it was written with the help of Silvanus, and sends greetings from "Babylon", which most readers have taken to mean Rome.
2-peter:
Second Peter is short, urgent and unlike the first letter in style — different enough that the early church debated whether to include it longer than for almost any other book. It is written as a last word: the author says he knows he must shortly put off this tabernacle, and wants what he has taught to be remembered after he is gone.

Its subject is teachers inside the church who deny what they were taught and live accordingly, and the second chapter describes them with a ferocity that has few parallels in the New Testament. Much of that chapter runs closely parallel to the letter of Jude, and which borrowed from which is an open question. The third chapter answers people asking where the promised coming has got to, and gives the reply that a day with the Lord is as a thousand years — and that the delay is patience, not failure.
1-john:
First John has no greeting, no named sender and no named recipients, which is why some read it as a sermon rather than a letter. It begins instead with a claim about evidence: that which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which our hands have handled. Something has happened in the community it addresses — people have left it — and the letter is written for those who stayed and are unsettled by it.

It circles rather than progresses, returning again and again to a small set of tests: whether someone keeps the commandments, whether they love their brother, whether they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. The vocabulary is very simple and the sentences are short, which makes it the passage most often given to new readers of Greek and deceptively easy in English. It is also the source of the flattest statement about God anywhere in scripture: God is love.
2-john:
Second John is thirteen verses, written on what was probably a single sheet, and it is addressed to "the elect lady and her children" — either an individual and her household or, more likely, a congregation spoken of as a woman. The writer calls himself only "the elder".

It does two things. It asks the readers to go on loving one another, which the writer notes is not a new commandment but the one they have had from the beginning. And it warns them about travelling teachers who do not confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, with instructions that sound harsh out of context: do not receive such a person into the house, or greet them. In a setting where visiting preachers depended on hospitality and a house was where the church met, receiving someone was closer to endorsing them. The elder ends by saying he would rather not write the rest, and hopes to come and speak face to face.
3-john:
Third John is the shortest book in the Bible, and it is a genuinely private letter — the only one in the New Testament addressed to a named individual about a specific local quarrel, with no doctrine in it at all. The elder writes to Gaius, whom he commends for taking in travelling missionaries who had gone out taking nothing from the Gentiles.

The trouble is a man named Diotrephes, who "loveth to have the preeminence", refuses to receive those same travellers, talks against the elder, and puts out of the church anyone who does receive them. There is no theological charge against him; the complaint is simply about how he behaves. A third man, Demetrius, is recommended. The letter ends as the second one does, with the writer saying he has much to write but will not do it with ink and pen.
jude:
Jude is twenty-five verses and says at the outset that it is not the letter its author meant to write. He had intended to write about the salvation they shared, and turned instead to something urgent: certain men had come into the church quietly, and he wanted it contested.

What follows is a rapid series of examples — Israel in the wilderness, the angels who left their estate, Sodom, Cain, Balaam, Korah — piled up rather than argued through. The letter is notable for citing sources outside the Old Testament: a dispute over the body of Moses, and a prophecy quoted directly from the book of Enoch. That, along with the long overlap with the second chapter of Second Peter, made it one of the books the early church was slowest to settle on. It closes with a benediction that has outlived every controversy about the rest of it.
revelation:
Revelation is the only book of its kind in the New Testament, and the kind has a name: apocalypse, meaning an unveiling. John writes from Patmos, an island he says he was on because of the word of God, and the book is framed as a letter — it opens with seven short, specific messages to seven real churches in Asia, each one naming what that congregation is doing well and what it is not.

After that it becomes vision, in sequences of seven, with numbers, colours, beasts and cities used as a language rather than as description. It draws constantly on Daniel, Ezekiel and Exodus without quoting them outright. Readers have interpreted it as a coded account of the Roman empire, as a map of church history, as a description of the end, and as a repeated pattern rather than a sequence; the argument is old and unlikely to close. The last two chapters set against all of it a city with no temple and no sun, and a promise that God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes.
